title: The Other End of the Trade
tagline: SPX options from the dealer's side of the trade, taught from the ground up: what a market maker takes on with every option, the hedging that forces on it, the footprint that hedging leaves on the index, and how to trade with that knowledge.
thesis: Every option ever traded created an obligation for someone to transact in the underlying. The market is, in part, the integral of those obligations.
blurb: Thirteen parts that build from returns and risk to the hedging a dealer is forced into, add that hedging up across the whole market, take the known sources of return one by one, and apply it all to trading SPX. Written for a reader new to markets, with the maths taught as it is needed and 54 interactive figures.
arc: How returns behave and how risk is measured: simple and log returns, the shape of a distribution, expected value, the Sharpe ratio and what it misses, drawdown, leverage, correlation, and the four places an edge can come from.

What you actually trade. “The S&P 500” is at least six products with their own settlement, taxes and trading hours, and beneath them sits the routing that decides who fills your order and at what cost.
Building a trading model, fitting it and testing it honestly: regression and classification, mean reversion and momentum, gradient descent, and how much to trade and how often.
Futures, swaps and options share one logic and differ mainly in their payoff. The part ends on why derivative markets exist at all.

The contract and its four basic positions, what an option’s price is made of, the Greeks of every order, volatility from daily moves to the implied surface, and put-call parity. Every later part assumes it.
Every option has a business on the other side of it: what that dealer inherits in the trade, how it neutralizes direction, and why gamma keeps undoing the hedge.
Why delta hedging is the correct strategy, derived in five steps to the Black-Scholes-Merton equation. A hedged option turns out to be a bet on realized volatility against implied.
From one dealer’s book to the market: gamma summed across strikes and expiries into gamma exposure, the two regimes it describes, and the episodes in which the framework broke.
The mechanism applied: the VIX as the same machinery seen from above, same-day options and what they have done to intraday volatility, and a classifier for reading the tape.
The known sources of return, each taken apart: the equity and variance risk premia, trend, carry, equity factors, calendar effects and regime filters, and the edges not worth trading.
How to swing-trade SPX, SPY and the largest stocks once the mechanics are known. The central claim is narrow: short-horizon mean reversion that holds only while specific, measurable conditions do.
About fifty-eight named option strategies, each reduced to its parts and sorted by difficulty, with margin and assignment at the end. Written to be looked up rather than read through.
The gap between paper and live results, and the discipline that closes it: the retail haircut, a conviction score, kill rules, worked examples, setup cards, the portfolio and its total vega.
The glossary, every formula on one page, the reading list and the one-page checklists.
